It is the form that produces a commitment rather than a mirror, and because it converts feeling into action it avoids the exhaustion that pure affective empathy causes in people who absorb distress all day.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges scoring a supervisor responding to a struggling employee award the answer that names the feeling and then commits to a specific change, not the one that only shares the distress.

terms.definition: The first 2.5% of a market to buy something new -- venturesome, able to absorb a failed purchase, and often socially outside the mainstream, which limits their influence; the early adopters who follow are the next 13.5% and carry the opinion leadership that actually moves the majority.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target at launch; quoting the 2.5% band and then explaining why that group cannot spread adoption alone is what separates the top scores.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: Latest allowable start minus earliest possible start for a task — the delay it can absorb before the project finish moves; total float is shared along a chain, whereas free float is the smaller amount that delays no immediately following task at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a network with early and late start dates, exam questions ask how long a task can slip; confusing the shared allowance with the task-level one over-promises the client in a status roleplay.

terms.definition: Earnings measured in what they buy rather than in dollars received: a 3% raise against 4% inflation is a cut of roughly 1%, since 1.03 divided by 1.04 comes to 0.99. The nominal number on the offer letter can rise every single year while this one falls, which is why a raise is judged against the inflation rate and not against last year's salary.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item giving a raise percentage and an inflation rate is asking for this comparison, and the trap answer is the one that calls any raise an improvement.

terms.definition: The parliamentary manual whose thresholds get tested: a main motion needs a second and passes on a simple majority of votes cast, an amendment needs a majority, closing debate by moving the previous question needs two-thirds because it takes away a member's right to speak, and a tie fails. Precedence governs order - while an amendment is pending, no new main motion is in order - and a point of order can interrupt because it concerns the rules rather than the question.
terms.whyItMatters: Officer and staff-meeting scenarios ask what vote a motion requires, and the two-thirds threshold for cutting off debate is the one competitors miss.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: Revenue attributable to a campaign divided by what that campaign cost: $40,000 of revenue on $10,000 of spend is 4.0. It differs from return on investment, which subtracts cost of goods and the spend itself before dividing, so a 4.0 here is still a losing campaign at a 20% gross margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A client presenting a campaign as a four-to-one success is the setup for this distinction; the competitor is expected to ask for the margin before agreeing the campaign made money.

terms.definition: Creating agreement and buy-in across a group with differing viewpoints.
terms.whyItMatters: It secures team alignment and commitment to shared decisions.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: Comparing budgeted cost of work actually completed against what was spent and what was planned: cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost, schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value, and any index below 1.0 signals over budget or behind schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-evaluation items ask whether a project that has spent sixty percent of its budget is in trouble; only the ratio against work completed answers it, and a raw spending percentage does not.

terms.definition: Written 30-, 60- or 90-day document listing measurable targets, the support the employer will provide and the stated consequence of missing them. It is not progressive discipline's verbal-then-written-warning ladder: discipline addresses conduct the employee chose, this addresses capability, and it doubles as the documentation trail for a for-cause termination.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervision roleplay about an employee who is trying hard and still missing quota calls for this, while a no-call-no-show calls for the discipline ladder instead.

terms.definition: A structured idea session run in four fixed stages: members write ideas silently and independently, then a round-robin in which each person contributes one idea per turn with no discussion allowed, then clarification of each posted item, then private ranking whose tally decides the outcome. Silent generation and one-at-a-time posting are what separate it from open brainstorming, where the loudest member anchors the room; the Delphi technique goes further by keeping experts anonymous across written rounds so they never meet at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Problem-solving group items ask which method protects the quiet member's idea, and this is the process that names how.

terms.definition: The Federal Trade Commission provision giving a buyer until midnight of the third business day to cancel a sale of $25 or more made at their home or anywhere other than the seller's permanent place of business, with the seller required to hand over two dated cancellation forms at signing. Sales made inside the seller's own store are not covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal and ethical selling items on the exam test the dollar threshold and the location condition, and in-home roleplays expect you to disclose the cancellation right rather than hurry the signature.

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: Bandura's task-specific confidence that you can carry out a particular action, built from four sources in descending order of power — a personal mastery experience, watching a similar person succeed, verbal persuasion, and how one reads one's own physical arousal. Self-esteem, by contrast, is a global judgment of personal worth, so a person can hold high esteem and low efficacy on one specific task.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking how a manager raises a nervous employee's confidence for a first presentation wants a staged small success rather than a pep talk, since mastery outranks persuasion.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: Inspecting a randomly drawn sample from a delivered lot and accepting or rejecting the entire lot on the count of defects found, against a stated acceptable quality level — the highest defect percentage treated as satisfactory — which trades a known risk of passing a bad lot for the cost of inspecting every unit.
terms.whyItMatters: Receiving-process questions ask how a buyer verifies a large shipment economically; naming the tolerable defect percentage and the risk it accepts is what distinguishes a full answer from 'check some of them'.

terms.definition: Seven-factor analysis the Department of Labor applies to decide whether an unpaid intern is really an employee: who gains the greater benefit, whether the work is tied to academic credit, whether it displaces paid staff, and whether either side expects a paid job at the end. If the employer is the main beneficiary, minimum wage and overtime are owed retroactively.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay staffing a startup with unpaid interns is scored on this test, because failing it turns free labor into back wages.

terms.definition: Federal law policing written warranties on consumer products: one costing more than $10 must be designated conspicuously as full or limited, terms must be available to read before purchase on products over $15, a full warranty may not shorten the duration of implied warranties, and issuing any written warranty strips the seller of the power to disclaim implied warranties. It also lets a prevailing consumer recover attorney fees, which is why small warranty claims get litigated at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays about extended service plans test whether a store that printed a warranty can still sell the item as is — under this Act it cannot.

terms.definition: Standard structures for business documents such as memos, reports, and proposals.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect the correct format for each document type.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.term: French and Raven's five bases of power
terms.definition: Distinguishes five sources of influence — legitimate power from the position, reward power, coercive power, expert power from demonstrated knowledge, and referent power from personal respect — with the first three attached to the role and the last two to the individual. Expert and referent power produce commitment; coercive power produces compliance only while someone is watching.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking a new team lead with no formal authority to get cooperation is scored on building expert and referent power, and exam items on using power appropriately turn on that split.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: Charting sample measurements over time against limits computed from the process's own variation to separate common-cause noise from assignable-cause shifts; it monitors a process while it runs, unlike acceptance sampling, which judges a finished lot after the fact.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality-method roleplays ask how to catch a drifting machine before it produces scrap; watching the charted trend is the in-process answer, and inspecting finished goods is the one judges mark as too late.

terms.definition: A retirement account whose contributions escape tax now and whose withdrawals are taxed later, trading a deduction today for taxable income in retirement.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement-planning roleplays turn on when the client wants the tax bill, which is the whole traditional-versus-Roth decision.

terms.definition: Minimum number of members who must be present for a body's votes to count — a majority of the membership under Robert's Rules unless the bylaws set something lower, often one third. Business conducted without one is void rather than merely defeated, so a motion that loses 3 to 2 stands as rejected while the same motion passed short of this number stands as nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A chapter-officer or board roleplay in which half the members skip the meeting is scored on whether the competitor recognizes that no decision can be made.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 index of how far a society's less powerful members accept unequal distribution of authority - Malaysia scores near 100, Austria near 11, the United States around 40. It is a separate dimension from individualism: a high-power-distance audience expects the most senior person to speak first, treats public disagreement with a manager as an attack, and takes an invitation to challenge the presenter as a trap, so a presentation that works in a low-index room must be restructured rather than merely translated.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to adapt a pitch for an overseas client, the scored answer changes who presents and how questions are invited, not just the language.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: Leading by modeling integrity, fairness, and moral principles.
terms.whyItMatters: It builds organizational trust and sets the tone for employee behavior.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: The process of finding and attracting qualified candidates for open positions.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective recruitment ensures a business has the talent to meet its needs.

terms.definition: Unloading inbound freight and transferring it directly to outbound trailers within hours, sorting by destination on the dock, so the goods are never put away — the opposite of conventional warehousing, which stores, picks and holds stock and therefore incurs carrying cost that this eliminates.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution roleplays about cutting inventory cost and speeding delivery expect this as the named technique, and the judge wants the requirement that inbound and outbound schedules be tightly synchronized.

terms.definition: Senior advocate who spends political capital on someone's behalf in rooms that person is not in, putting their name into promotion and staffing decisions and absorbing reputational risk if it goes badly. A mentor spends time instead of capital — advice given directly to you, with nothing of the mentor's own staked on the outcome.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on advancement patterns is scored on this distinction, because the competitor who only asks for coffee chats never gets named in the promotion meeting.

terms.definition: A readability formula that grades a passage as 0.4 x (words per sentence + percentage of words carrying three or more syllables), so it counts only 'hard words' instead of weighting every syllable the way Flesch-Kincaid does. On the same paragraph the two scores diverge whenever long sentences are built from plain words: a 40-word sentence of one-syllable words drives fog up sharply while Flesch-Kincaid barely moves. General business writing is normally targeted at 12 or below and news writing near 11.
terms.whyItMatters: An editing item hands you one paragraph and two readability scores and asks which formula flagged it, and a roleplay defending a rewritten warranty is scored on naming a target number rather than promising the draft now 'reads better.'

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.

terms.definition: Models trustworthiness as credibility plus reliability plus intimacy, all divided by self-orientation — so visibly acting in your own interest divides away everything the other three terms earn. Credibility is about words, reliability about repeated actions over time, and intimacy about safety in disclosure, which is why a person can be believable and still not be trusted.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on rebuilding a client or coworker relationship is scored on lowering the self-orientation term — leading with their problem — rather than on producing more credentials.

terms.definition: A systematic review of external conditions, competitor activity, and market trends.
terms.whyItMatters: Scanning the environment lets competitors spot opportunities and threats before deciding.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: Boundaries drawn three standard deviations above and below the process mean and calculated FROM the process's own output, which makes them a statement of what the process does — specification limits are set by the customer or engineer and state what the product must be, so a process can sit inside one pair and outside the other.
terms.whyItMatters: The classic exam trap shows points inside the charted band but outside customer tolerance; recognizing that a stable process can still be producing unacceptable parts is the tested discrimination.

terms.definition: Prompt demanding a specific past incident, on the premise that past behavior predicts future behavior, with answers scored against written anchors — which is why a hypothetical answer earns zero. A situational question does the opposite, asking what you would do in a scenario you have never faced, and is scored for reasoning rather than evidence.
terms.whyItMatters: The interview portion of a job-seeking roleplay is graded on giving a dated, quantified incident when the question asks for one, not a description of your general habits.

terms.definition: The medium — email, phone, in person, memo — chosen for a message.
terms.whyItMatters: Justifying channel choice signals professional maturity.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: Any contact at which a buyer forms a judgment about a brand with no marketing message present to help — Procter & Gamble named the 3 to 7 seconds facing the shelf the first such moment and the first use of the product the second; the practical rule is that advertising spend cannot repair a touchpoint at which the customer has already decided against the brand.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about check-in or complaint handling are scored on identifying the exact contact that decides the guest's opinion and fixing that, not on adding promotion.

terms.definition: The work of managing your own feelings to satisfy an employer's display rules — the face the job requires — and it is performed two ways: surface acting, which puts on the expression while the underlying feeling is unchanged, and deep acting, which alters the felt emotion itself. Surface acting is the strategy repeatedly tied to higher exhaustion and turnover; deep acting is not.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on staffing a long shift of difficult interactions is scored on recognizing that requiring a constant smile is a real cost to be scheduled around, not a free instruction.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: Amplification of demand variability moving upstream, where a small retail sales swing becomes a larger distributor order swing and a still larger factory order swing, driven by batch ordering, price promotions, forecast updating and shortage gaming — shared point-of-sale data damps it.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain collaboration roleplays use this to justify sharing real sales data with suppliers, and the four named causes are what turn a vague answer about 'communication' into a scored one.

terms.definition: Cover document sent with an application to a posted opening, naming the requisition and tying two or three of its stated requirements to specific evidence from your record. A letter of inquiry does the same job for a company with no advertised opening, so it opens with the employer's problem instead of with a listing.
terms.whyItMatters: A written-event or job-search roleplay that supplies a job posting expects the letter to answer that posting's requirements point by point.

terms.definition: Scores a passage from 0 to 100 where a HIGHER number means easier, running opposite in direction to every grade-level formula: 206.835 - 1.015 x (words per sentence) - 84.6 x (syllables per word). The 60-to-70 band is the plain-English range consumer documents target, 30 and below is college-graduate difficulty, and 90-100 is fifth-grade text. Because the scale runs to 100, a score of 70 is good here while a grade-level score of 70 would be absurd.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items and written-event judges both hand you a score and ask whether the document suits its audience; reading this 0-to-100 scale as though it were a grade level reverses your answer.

terms.definition: Adams's model in which an employee compares their own outcome-to-input ratio against a referent other's ratio and, when the two ratios differ, restores balance by cutting effort, demanding more reward, or changing the comparison target; perceived fairness, not absolute pay, drives the response.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a well-paid employee who resents a colleague's raise are scored on the ratio comparison and on which restoration behavior to expect.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: Fisher and Ury's method built on four rules — separate the people from the problem, focus on interests instead of stated positions, invent options for mutual gain before deciding anything, and insist on an objective standard for the outcome. A position is what a party demands; the interest is why they want it, and only the interest can usually be satisfied in more than one way.
terms.whyItMatters: Negotiation roleplays are scored on surfacing the reason behind a demand and offering two options that meet it, which positional haggling over one number cannot produce.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: The width of the customer's tolerance divided by six standard deviations of process spread, with Cpk penalizing an off-center mean by measuring only the nearer specification limit; 1.33 is the common minimum and a value below 1.0 means defects are unavoidable even when the process is perfectly stable.
terms.whyItMatters: Supplier-quality roleplays use this figure as the acceptance bar: a supplier can hold a steady process and still fail, which is the argument you make when resolving a quality dispute.

terms.definition: The information return a business files for every non-employee it paid $600 or more for services in a calendar year, furnished to both the worker and the IRS by January 31. Nothing is withheld, so the contractor carries the whole 15.3% self-employment tax (12.4% Social Security + 2.9% Medicare) and pays it in quarterly estimates, whereas a Form W-2 employee splits that load with an employer paying 7.65%; a payee who supplies no taxpayer ID triggers 24% backup withholding.
terms.whyItMatters: Career-cluster exam items ask what changes when a firm hires a freelance designer instead of a staff one, and a professional-development roleplay where the judge plays a first-time gig worker is graded on naming the $600 filing trigger and the fact that no tax comes out of the check.

terms.definition: Two firms at the SAME channel stage pooling capital, production or distribution to chase an opportunity neither could take alone — a coffee brand operating kiosks inside a bookstore chain. A vertical marketing system, by contrast, joins firms at DIFFERENT stages of the same channel under one owner, contract or dominant member.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurship and marketing roleplays that propose a co-branded partnership are graded on naming this structure and the fact that neither partner is the other's supplier.

terms.definition: Letter layout that keeps the inside address, salutation, body paragraphs and any lists flush at the left margin but starts the dateline, complimentary close and signature block at the horizontal center of the page - about the 3-inch tab on a page with 1-inch margins. That one shifted column is the only difference from full block; adding a half-inch first-line indent to every paragraph converts it again into semi-block.
terms.whyItMatters: Formatting questions show the same letter three ways and score the competitor who can point to which elements moved, rather than judging the page by how balanced it looks.

terms.definition: Lapsed customers who return after a targeted campaign, divided by lapsed customers contacted — 120 of 2,000 is 6%. It usually beats new acquisition on cost because the contact data and purchase history are already owned, but only when the offer answers the stated reason for leaving rather than simply discounting the same product.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay asks which list gets the budget, and this rate weighed against customer acquisition cost is the comparison judges expect.

terms.definition: Short for best alternative to a negotiated agreement: the course of action you would actually take if these talks failed, which is what sets real bargaining power. It is not the price target and not the reservation price — the reservation price is the worst deal still worth accepting, derived from the alternative — and improving the outside option raises your power even if nothing at the table changes.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier or salary negotiation roleplay is scored on the candidate knowing their walk-away option and estimating the other side's before conceding.

terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Unit price plus freight, insurance, duties and tariffs, customs brokerage, and handling to the receiving dock — the total that makes an offshore quote comparable to a domestic one, which is why the lower quoted unit price frequently loses once every downstream charge is added.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays present a cheaper overseas bid and expect you to reject a comparison based on quoted price alone by adding the delivery-related charges before deciding.

terms.definition: Scales a controlled market's result to a national number by dividing the test volume by that market's share of national category volume — 60,000 units in a market holding 2% of national volume projects to 3,000,000 units — then discounting for support levels, distribution or pricing that cannot be repeated nationwide.
terms.whyItMatters: Rollout questions give the test units plus the market's percentage of national volume and expect the projection; the discount step is what a judge presses on when a plan's national number looks suspiciously clean.

terms.definition: Software that parses every application into structured fields and ranks candidates by keyword match against the requisition before a recruiter reads a single one. Multi-column layouts, text inside images and invented section headings are dropped during parsing, so a qualified candidate can be screened out by formatting rather than by qualifications.
terms.whyItMatters: A job-search roleplay advising a competitor whose applications get no response usually turns on this filter, not on the strength of the experience.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' pole opposite universalism: which rule applies depends on the relationship and the circumstance, so a signed contract is a starting point a long-standing partner may reopen, and an obligation to a friend can outrank written policy. Universalist cultures - the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Germany - hold that one standard binds everyone regardless of who is asking, which is why the identical request reads as reasonable flexibility on one side of the table and as favoritism on the other.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay where a long-time distributor asks for terms no other account receives is scored on naming the cultural logic at work before ruling on the request.

terms.definition: A refund, credit or replacement granted where the company owes nothing contractually — outside warranty, past the return window, or where the customer caused the damage. It is expensed as a service or marketing cost rather than charged against the warranty reserve, which is why finance tracks it separately and caps each agent's authority in dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the customer's claim is genuinely out of policy tests whether the competitor can grant an exception and state what it costs the company.

terms.definition: Over-weighting a person's character and under-weighting their circumstances when explaining someone else's behavior — the late colleague is careless rather than stuck behind an accident. Its mirror image applied to oneself is the self-serving bias, and together the pair make an appraisal reward good luck and punish bad context.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking why a supervisor rates a rep poorly after a territory loses its largest account expects this bias by name, and roleplays on fair evaluation reward asking about conditions before judging the person.

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: Distance of one observation from the mean measured in standard deviations, (x minus the mean) divided by the standard deviation, so a store running 2.5 standard deviations above average scores 2.5 whether sales are in units or dollars; it is what lets two measures on different scales be ranked on one ruler, and it is negative below the mean.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing a store's traffic performance with its basket-size performance requires putting both on the same standardized scale before either can be called the bigger outlier.

terms.definition: An international quality-management standard certifying that documented processes exist, are followed and are audited by an independent registrar with surveillance visits — it certifies the management SYSTEM, not the product, so a registered firm can lawfully make a mediocre item consistently.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays treat registration as evidence of process discipline, and the judge is listening for the caveat that it guarantees consistency rather than excellence.

terms.definition: A route into a second state's professional licence that accepts a licence already held in good standing elsewhere — for CPAs, commonly practice in four of the last ten years plus education and exam requirements the receiving board judges substantially equivalent — instead of requiring the applicant to sit that state's own examination again. It runs one direction only, which is what separates it from reciprocity: the receiving state grants the privilege and the sending state owes nothing in return.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay in which the judge plays an accountant relocating for a promotion turns on whether they must re-test, and exam items on advancement patterns expect this route named rather than a vague 'get licensed again.'

terms.definition: The identity and reputation a person projects through their online presence.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal social media brand can boost or damage credibility.

terms.definition: The share of customers who buy again inside a defined window, counted per purchase occasion — 30 of 100 first-time buyers ordering again within 90 days is 30%. Retention rate counts customers still active at period end whether or not they bought anything, so a subscription can post 95% retention alongside a repurchase rate of zero.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty cases mix the two constantly, and naming the difference in the denominator is the discriminating answer a judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Scott's grid crossing caring personally with challenging directly: high on both is candor, caring without challenging is ruinous empathy that withholds the correction that would have helped, challenging without caring is obnoxious aggression, and neither is manipulative insincerity. The named failure most managers actually commit is the first, not harshness.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a well-liked employee is quietly underperforming is scored on delivering the specific correction, since softening it to protect the relationship is the graded mistake.

terms.definition: The knife-edge case where the coefficient equals exactly 1: a 10% price cut brings a 10% volume gain and total revenue does not move at all. Above 1 demand is elastic and revenue moves opposite to price; below 1 it is inelastic and revenue moves with price.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a matched pair of percentages and ask what happens to revenue, and recognizing this case rather than assuming revenue rises is the trap being tested.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: A control that releases payment only when the purchase order, the receiving report and the supplier invoice agree on item, quantity and price; any one document alone can be forged or wrong, so requiring all three is what blocks payment for goods never ordered or never delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounts-payable and ethics-in-purchasing roleplays ask what stops a fraudulent invoice from being paid, and naming all three documents plus the fields compared is the complete answer.

terms.definition: Degree program alternating full-time paid work terms with academic terms, where the work terms carry academic credit and a faculty evaluation. An internship is a single standalone placement with no required academic component, which is why students on this track often graduate with a year or more of documented, evaluated experience.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on ways to build work experience while still in school is scored on distinguishing the credit-bearing alternating program from a one-off summer job.

terms.definition: A gesture carrying a fixed verbal translation that works with no speech at all - a thumbs-up, a head shake, the finger-and-thumb ring - which is precisely what separates it from an illustrator, a gesture that means nothing apart from the words it accompanies, such as sketching a package's size in the air. Because the translation is assigned by culture rather than by resemblance, this type can invert across a border: the same ring means money in Japan and is obscene in Brazil.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay that has you demonstrate a product to a foreign buyer is scored on choosing gestures whose meaning does not flip, and exam items ask which gesture type still communicates when used silently.

terms.definition: A published schedule matching the size of the failure to the size of the fix — apology plus correction for a minor first delay, a partial credit of roughly 10% to 25% of the transaction for a repeat, and a full refund plus a retention offer where the failure cost the customer money. It keeps compensation consistent and stops the loudest complainer being paid the most.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges in complaint roleplays reward a proportionate remedy; naming the rung and its value beats offering a blanket refund every time.

terms.definition: The 13.5% of buyers who follow the innovators -- respected opinion leaders inside the mainstream whose endorsement decides whether an item reaches the 34% early majority; innovators, the first 2.5%, buy sooner but sit too far outside the group to persuade it.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion plans for a launch are scored on targeting the group that others watch; naming the 13.5% band and its opinion-leader role answers the indicator directly.

terms.definition: Gable's strongest of four ways to answer someone's good news, formed by crossing active with passive and constructive with destructive: responding actively and constructively means asking questions that let the person relive the event, while passive-constructive is a flat nice job, active-destructive points out the downside, and passive-destructive changes the subject. Only the first strengthens the relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays on recognizing a team member's contribution are scored on a specific, curious response in the moment rather than a generic congratulation or a deferred award.
